chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadeed, from Jameel, from one of our companions, from one of the two (Imams) (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who bought a sacrificial animal and slaughtered it. A man passed by and recognized it, and said: 'This is my she-camel that strayed from me yesterday.' And two men testified to that. He (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Its meat is for him, and it does not suffice for either of the two (as a sacrifice).' Then he (peace be upon him) said: 'And due to that, the Sunnah is established with marking it and yoking it when it is recognized.'

key_terms.إِشْعَارِهَا: Marking it (with a mark to identify it)
key_terms.تَقْلِيدِهَا: Yoking it (putting a ring in its nose)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a sacrificial animal is claimed by its original owner after being slaughtered?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the ruling for a sacrificial animal (hady) claimed by its original owner after slaughter, where the Imam declares the meat belongs to the claimant but the sacrifice is invalid for both parties. This necessitates that each individual offer a new sacrifice, illustrating the principle of 'ishtar' (marking/identifying) as the Sunnah for establishing ownership in such disputes. The ruling underscores the importance of clear identification in ritual obligations, a concept deeply rooted in Shia jurisprudence regarding property rights and ritual validity.
